title: Learn a Local Dance
goal: Your kid learns a traditional dance from someone who keeps it, where you're travelling or from your family's own roots. They ask what the dance is for, find the count hiding in its music, break the moves into a map they can practise in small chunks, then tell its story and perform it for family.
need: Someone who knows a traditional dance: a teacher, a cultural centre, a festival workshop or a grandparent
The dance's music, recorded or on a phone (ask the teacher which song)
Room to move: furniture pushed back, a yard or a park

levelsLine: Every step has three levels: Explore, Develop, Extend. Pick the one that fits your kid today, and change it anytime. Siblings can do the same step at different levels, side by side.

howTo.intro: Your part is the introductions and the courage. Find the person who knows the dance, ask whether it's one you're welcome to learn, then dance beside your kid at every lesson and practice, wobbly steps included, so the first tries belong to both of you.

plan.what: Find the dance and its keeper (Step 1).
Ask for its story and find the count (Steps 2 and 3).
Map the moves, then perform it (Steps 4 and 5).

troubleshoot.a: Ask the oldest relatives you can reach what they danced at weddings and festivals. Look for a cultural association from your family's roots, or a ceilidh or barn dance night, where a caller usually walks beginners through each dance first.
Turn the music off. Say the counts out loud at half speed until the feet know the way, then add the music back for one chunk at a time.
Perform side by side with them, or for one person first. Let them start with the story, which gives them a minute to settle before the first step.

lesson.text: A traditional dance is a pattern of moves laid over a count, and kept for a reason: a wedding, a harvest, a festival, a way of saying who you are. Once you can hear the count and see the moves as small pieces, almost anyone can learn it.
lesson.before: 'I can't dance. I just don't have rhythm.'

model.line: The music goes in 3. Clapped ONE two three until it felt easy.
Four moves, each drawn as footprints with its counts underneath.
Move 1 alone, then 1 and 2, then all four, slowly and without music.
Told the family it's a wedding dance, then danced it with the music.

lesson.modelNote: 'No rhythm' turned out to be no count. Once the music had numbers and the dance had a map, every step had a place to land, and the kid who had 'no rhythm' danced it start to finish.

steps.title: Find the dance and its keeper
steps.why: A dance learned from a person comes with the corrections, the stories and the welcome that a video can't give.
steps.kid: Your kid looks for a traditional dance from where you are, or from your family's roots, using the Find the dance card in the Local Dance Toolkit at the end of the guide. They find someone who knows it, a teacher, a cultural centre, a festival workshop or a grandparent, and ask if it's one visitors can learn.
steps.you: Make the first contact, and offer to pay for a lesson. If a dance belongs to a ceremony or to certain people only, watch it with respect and choose a social dance instead.
ask: Who here, or in our family, still dances the old way?
Is this a dance anyone is welcome to learn?
steps.tip: Dances for weddings, village festivals and community nights are often the ones meant for everyone to join.

levels.explore: Watch a dance with a parent, and point to the move you'd most like to try.
levels.develop: Find a dance and someone who can teach it, and ask if visitors may learn it.
levels.extend: Find out which dances here are for everyone and which are kept for ceremonies or certain people, and why that difference matters.

steps.title: Ask for its story
steps.why: Every move was kept for a reason. Knowing it changes how you dance it.
steps.kid: Before or during the first lesson, your kid asks the person teaching about the dance, using the Ask the dancer card: when people dance it, what it celebrates, what the moves mean and how it has changed. They write the answers in a notebook as the dance's story.
steps.you: Learn a few polite words in the local language if you need them, then let your kid do the asking. Take the lesson yourself, beside them, not from the bench.
ask: When do people dance this, and why?
Does any move copy something real, like work, animals or a story?
steps.tip: Ask about the clothes, the music and any shouts or claps too. A dance is more than the feet.

levels.explore: Ask one question about the dance, and draw what it's for.
levels.develop: Ask three questions from the card, and write the dance's story in a notebook.
levels.extend: Find a second dance from the same place for a different occasion, and compare what each one is for.

steps.title: Find the count
steps.why: Every dance sits on a count. Once you can hear it, the steps have somewhere to land.
steps.kid: Your kid listens to the dance's music and claps the beat, then finds the strong beat that starts each group, using the Count the music card. They count it out loud: in 2s, 3s, 4s or 6s, or in 7 like the Greek kalamatianos, slow, quick, quick.
steps.you: Clap with them. Ask the teacher which song goes with the dance, and whether you may record it to practise with later.
ask: Where does the strong beat land?
Is this music counted in 2, 3, 4 or something else?
steps.tip: Clap on every beat, then stamp only on the 1. When the stamp feels easy, you've found the count.

levels.explore: Clap along to the music, and stamp your foot when the beat feels strong.
levels.develop: Find the count, and say it out loud through the whole song.
levels.extend: Clap the count of a favourite song from home, try one move of the dance to it, and work out whether it fits, and why or why not.

steps.title: Map the moves
steps.why: A dance is easier to learn as a few small chunks than as one long blur.
steps.kid: Your kid breaks the dance into moves and draws a move map, using the Move map card: each move as footprints or a stick figure, with its counts underneath. Then they practise one chunk at a time, slowly and without music, and add the next only when the first feels easy.
steps.you: Learn it beside them and say the counts out loud together. Make mistakes too, and laugh at them. Show the map to the teacher if you can, so they can fix it.
ask: Which move is hardest to remember?
How many counts does one full round take?
steps.tip: Practise in short bursts, 10 minutes a day for a few days, rather than once for an hour.

levels.explore: Learn the first move with a parent, and say its counts out loud.
levels.develop: Draw the full move map, and dance it through at half speed.
levels.extend: Circle where the dance repeats on your map, and work out how many rounds fit in the whole song.

steps.title: Perform it for family
steps.why: Dancing it for people who love you turns practice into something you did.
steps.kid: Your kid plans a show night, using the Show night card. They tell the audience the dance's story and who taught it, perform it with the music, then answer the audience's questions. Then they write in a notebook: the dance, the teacher, the place and the date.
steps.you: Ask the teacher if it's all right to show the dance, and to share a video with family. Dance as their partner if they want one, and clap loudest at the end.
ask: What do you want the audience to know before you start?
What would your teacher say about how you danced it?
steps.tip: Grandparents far away can watch on a video call. Some will remember a dance of their own.

levels.explore: Dance one chunk for family, with a parent beside you.
levels.develop: Tell the dance's story, then perform the whole dance with the music.
levels.extend: Ask a family member to teach you a dance they grew up with, map it the same way, and compare its count with yours.

conclusion.headline: They danced a tradition someone trusted them with.
conclusion.text: Put on any song in the kitchen a week from now. Clapping for the 1 in music they never danced to shows they learned to listen, not only to move.
conclusion.celebrate: When the music stops after the show, say: 'Someone who keeps this dance taught it to you, and you carried it all the way here.'
extensions: Find how the same dance is done in a nearby town or by families who moved abroad, and spot what changed
Teach the first chunk to a friend using only your move map, and see where the map needs fixing
Find out what the dancers' clothes are made of and why, and how they move when the dance does
Find the instrument that keeps the beat in the dance's music, and ask someone to show you how it's played

signs: They clap for the 1 in songs without being asked
They ask what a dance is for before joining it
They break a hard thing into small chunks to learn it
makeItReal: Pick a day in the next month, like a birthday or a family video call, to dance it for someone new, and put it on the calendar with your kid today.
